Wednesday, November 4th, 2026¶

Last class, we discussed using the mean and/or median filters to remove salt and pepper noise.

In [2]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

We worked with some sample images from the course webpage, and converted them to grayscale.

In [3]:
circuit = plt.imread('circuit.png')
gray_circuit = np.mean(circuit, axis=2) # Convert the RGB circuit array to 2D grayscale
In [ ]:
padded_circuit = get_padded_img(gray_circuit, 3)

We then added salt and pepper noise to these images.

In [4]:
noisy_circuit = gray_circuit.copy()   # Initialize noisy_img as a 2D grayscale array
nrows, ncols = noisy_circuit.shape

r = np.random.random((nrows, ncols))  # Array of the same shape as noisy_img full of random floats
                                      # between 0 and 1.

salt_mask =   r > .9 # Identify 10% of entries that will be hit with salt noise
pepper_mask = r < .1 # Identify 10% of entries that will be hit with pepper noise

noisy_circuit[salt_mask]   = 1 # Add salt noise
noisy_circuit[pepper_mask] = 0 # Add pepper noise

We then applied the mean/median filter using 3 by 3 grids and ignoring any edge pixels.

In [5]:
median_filtered_circuit = noisy_circuit.copy()
mean_filtered_circuit = noisy_circuit.copy()
nrows, ncols = noisy_circuit.shape

for i in range(1,nrows-1):     # For every row other than the first and last
    for j in range(1,ncols-1): # For every column other than the first and last
        grid = noisy_circuit[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2]     # Build a 3x3 grid centered at pixel i,j
        grid_median = np.median(grid)
        grid_mean = np.mean(grid)
        mean_filtered_circuit[i,j] = grid_mean     # Set i,j-th filtered pixel to mean of the 3x3 grid
        median_filtered_circuit[i,j] = grid_median # Set i,j-th filtered pixel to median of the 3x3 grid

Dealing with edge pixels¶

With the simple filters written above, we have ignored filtering pixels along the edge of the image. Let's try to deal with them now.

The project page discusses adding extra rows/columns to our array so that we are able to construct a 3 by 3 grid centered at all pixels of our original image.

If we are using 3 by 3 grids, we need to add one extra row/column on all sides. Our strategy then is to:

  • Create an array padded_img that has two additional rows and two additional columns than the noisy_img array;
  • Place the contents of the noisy_img array into a slice of the padded_img array that skips the first and last rows and first and last columns;
  • Apply the the mean/median filter to each of the non-edge pixels of the padded_img (which corresponds to applying the filter to every pixel of the noisy_img array).
In [8]:
noisy_img = noisy_circuit.copy()
nrows, ncols = noisy_img.shape
In [9]:
padded_img = np.zeros((nrows + 2, ncols + 2))  # Create a new array with 2 extra rows and 2 extra columns

padded_img[1:-1, 1:-1] = noisy_img     # Set the original noisy_img array into the interior of padded_img
In [ ]:

Let's take a closer look at one corner of the padded_img array:

In [10]:
plt.imshow(padded_img[:10,:10], cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=1)
Out[10]:
<matplotlib.image.AxesImage at 0x1e447c03250>
In [ ]:

Now, we want to use the padded_img array to build our 3 by 3 grids for computing means/medians. Let's copy in our median filter code and make any necessary changes.

In [11]:
median_filtered_img = noisy_img.copy()
nrows, ncols = noisy_img.shape

for i in range(nrows):     # For every row 
    for j in range(ncols): # For every column
        grid = padded_img[i:i+3, j:j+3]        # Build a 3x3 grid center on pixel i,j of noisy_img
        grid_median = np.median(grid)
        median_filtered_img[i,j] = grid_median # Set i,j-th filtered pixel to median of the 3x3 grid
In [13]:
plt.imshow(median_filtered_img, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=1)
plt.axis('off') # This will remove x and y ticks and labels
Out[13]:
(np.float64(-0.5), np.float64(639.5), np.float64(425.5), np.float64(-0.5))
In [ ]:

Note: We have added black border to the padded_img (since we used np.zeros), which propogates into the filtered_img when we take any mean that includes padded pixels. We could instead add a white border (by using np.ones), but that's not any better. We could split the difference by using np.ones(...)/2 to use a gray border. For the project, it might be a good idea to think of other ways that one could deal with filtering pixels along the edges.

Let's try to turn the sample code above into some functions that we can use more broadly.
